Cadmium(II) adsorption by recyclable Zeolite-Loaded Hydrogel: Extension [![](data:image/png;base64,)](http://crossmark.crossref.org/dialog/?doi=10.1016/j.cej.2024.151842&domain=pdf) to the removal of Cadmium(II) from contaminated soil

A R T I C L E I N F O

_Keywords:_ Zeolite Hydrogel

Adsorption mechanism Soil remediation Cd(II) reduction

A B S T R A C T

Excessive cadmium(II) (Cd(II)) in soil has gravely jeopardized global ecosystem stability and human health. The removal of Cd(II) is a permanent cure to remediate Cd(II)-contaminated soil. Herein, a recyclable removal material, zeolite@cellulose-poly(acrylamide) hydrogel (Z@CA) was developed. Batch adsorption experiments and characterisations (SEM-EDS, FTIR, XRD, and XPS) were conducted to explore the adsorption capacity and mechanism of Z@CA. A pot experiment was established to evaluate the effect of Z@CA on soil Cd(II) remediation and Cd(II) toxicity in water spinach. The results showed that in aqueous solutions, the maximum adsorption capacity of Cd(II) by Z@CA was 84.4 mg⋅g—1. Electrostatic attraction, ion exchange, and surface complexation collectively facilitated Cd(II) capture by Z@CA. Even after five adsorption–desorption cycles, Z@CA maintained a Cd(II) removal efficiency of 89.88%. The results of the pot experiment showed that after applying Z@CA (2.5 w/w) in soil for 21 days, the content of bioavailable Cd(II) and total Cd(II) significantly decreased by 59.38% and 1.75%, respectively. The recovery rate of Z@CA reached 94.77% and maintained its original intact structure. In addition, the Cd(II) content of water spinach was reduced by 91.43% compared to the treatment without Z@CA, the weight, height, and relative chlorophyll content reaching 1.34, 1.73, and 1.49 times that of the treatment without Z@CA. The ideal application of Z@CA provides novel approaches and insights into the remediation of Cd (II)-contaminated soils.

# Introduction

Cadmium(II), a ubiquitous contaminant, is primarily generated through intensive anthropogenic activities and discharge, including mining, smelting, underground space development, and unsustainable agricultural practices [\[1–4\]](#_bookmark14). Cd(II) in the soil is simple to accumulate but challenging to degrade. It is readily transferred from soil to plants and enters the human food chain, causing irreversible and severe damage to the kidneys, liver, bones, and other organs [\[5,6\]](#_bookmark15). Therefore, remediation of Cd(II)-contaminated soils is urgently required. Passivation is a well-developed technique for remediating soils contaminated with heavy metals [\[7\]](#_bookmark16). It typically refers to the modification of soil physicochemical properties or the direct adsorption of heavy metals by introducing pas-sivators, thereby reducing the bioavailability of heavy metals [\[8\]](#_bookmark17). As discovered by Wang et al [\[9\]](#_bookmark18), after four weeks of applying the sludge biochar passivator, the soil DTPA-Cd(II), Pb(II) and Zn(II) reduced by

3.1%, 4.8% and 9.8%, respectively, and the NH4OAc-Cd(II), Pb(II) and Zn(II) reduced by 19.0%, 14.2% and 8.0%, respectively. However, the effective removal of heavy metals cannot be achieved through passiv-ation remediation [\[10\]](#_bookmark19). More seriously, once the soil environment is altered, immobilized heavy metals may be remobilized, causing sec-ondary pollution [\[11\]](#_bookmark20). From the perspective of agricultural sustain-ability, recycling the applied passivation materials after use could directly remove heavy metals from the soil. In other words, endowing passivation materials with recoverability is the key to eradicating Cd(II)-contaminated soil.

Nowadays, there is a proliferation of novel remediation materials targeting heavy metals. For example, Azam et al. [\[12\]](#_bookmark21) prepared cost-effective adsorbents based on ajwa date pits to remove heavy metals from aqueous medium. A novel biomass prepared from fungal isolates including, Penicillium chrysogenum and Aspergillus ustus could also be utilized for the removal of heavy metals [\[13\]](#_bookmark22). However, despite

demonstrating promising application efficacy in aqueous environments, the prospects of these remediation materials in soil remain uncertain. In contrast, zeolite, a natural aluminosilicate mineral, has been widely used for Cd(II)-contaminated soil attributed to its enhanced adsorption capacity, crystalline structural stability, and favourable environmental compatibility [\[14\]](#_bookmark23). Its practical application can mitigate the toxicity and potential environmental risks posed by Cd(II) in soil. For instance, Rahmany-Saman et al [\[15\]](#_bookmark24) revealed that applying natural zeolite re-duces the Cd(II) concentrations by 24.1% in the seed; 26.7% in the stem and leaf; 16.5% in the soil. Feng et al [\[16\]](#_bookmark25) found that after the appli-cation of zeolite in the soil, the content of exchangeable Cd(II) decreased significantly and the content of iron manganese oxide bound Cd(II) increased significantly at the same time. Ma et al [\[17\]](#_bookmark26) reported that upon the addition of 10% of modified zeolite, the weak acid extracted forms of Cd(II) in the soil were reduced by 10%. Therefore, finding suitable recovery carriers for zeolites may be an effective way to achieve the reduction of Cd(II) in soil.

Hydrogels are ideal recyclable carriers for passivation materials.

Hydrogels are materials with a three-dimensional framework structure formed by the dissolution of macromolecules within water [\[18\]](#_bookmark27). They are usually “jelly-like” solids with an elastic nature, and the shape and size can be adjusted according to the preparation mould [\[19\]](#_bookmark28). Simul-taneously, hydrogels can swell but are insoluble in water and offer a large pore size for the mass transport of water and ions [\[20\]](#_bookmark29). Hydrogels also contain a large number of hydrophilic groups such as carboxyl and hydroxyl, which can provide binding sites for heavy metals [\[21\]](#_bookmark30). Nevertheless, the mechanical properties of traditional hydrogels are not prominent, they are easily broken when subjected to external forces,

tetramethylethylenediamine (TMEDA), and other reagents were pur-chased from Macklin Biochemistry Science and Technology Co. Ltd (Shanghai, China). Potassium persulfate (KSP) was purchased from Baishi Chemical Co. Ltd (Tianjin, China). Sodium nitrate (NaOH) and nitric acid (HNO)3 were purchased from Guangzhou Chemical Reagent Factory (Guangzhou, China). Cd(NO)3⋅4H2O was purchased from Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd (Shanghai, China). All the chemicals were used as supplied. All pure water used was deionized water (DI water, 18.2 MΩ⋅cm—1) produced by a laboratory water purifier (Direct 8, Milli-Q, USA).

- 1.  _Preparation of Z@CA hydrogels_

Z@CA was prepared through a one-pot method. The zeolite was uniformly dispersed in deionized water (100 mL). AM, MAH, and NMBA were sequentially added at a predetermined temperature and stirred thoroughly at a specific stirring rate. The pH of the solution was adjusted to 4—5 using 5 mol⋅L—1 NaOH. CMC was added, and the pH was further adjusted to neutral. KSP and TMEDA were then added to the solution, which was vigorously stirred and thoroughly mixed. Subsequently, the mixture was poured into a mold and left to solidify. Once solidified, the resulting material was washed with deionized water in sequence three times, and dried at 60 ◦C for 48 h to obtain the final product Z@CA.

Hydrogels composed of acrylamide and cellulose without added zeolite were also prepared and denoted as CA. The zeolite-loaded mass ratio of Z@CA was calculated using Eq. [(1)](#_bookmark3), where m is the mass of CA after drying to a constant weight and M is the mass of the zeolite.

served as a functional building block to endow hydrogel with sufficient mechanical strength. Thus, Hydrogel loaded with zeolite might be able to avoid defects of weak mechanical properties ingeniously, promoting the application of hydrogel in the soil. However, to the best of our knowledge, studies on zeolite-loaded hydrogel for the removal of heavy metals from soil have not been reported up to now.

Therefore, in this study, a recyclable removal material, zeolite@cellulose-poly(acrylamide) hydrogels (Z@CA) was prepared. The loading of zeolite not only improved the mechanical strength of the hydrogel but also solved the problem of its difficult recycling as a passivation material. Batch adsorption experiments were conducted to elucidate the effects of pH, contact time, and initial concentration on Cd

(II) removal. Scanning electron microscopy equipped with an energy dispersive spectroscope (SEM-EDS), Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectra, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) were used to investigate the adsorption mechanism of Z@CA on Cd(II). The adsorption-removal potential of Z@CA in Cd(II)-contaminated soil was confirmed through pot experiments. These findings provide new ap-proaches and suggestions for the remediation of heavy metal-contaminated soils.

# Experimental

- 1.  _Chemicals and materials_

The zeolite used in this study was synthesized according to a previ-ous study by our team [\[25\]](#_bookmark33) and was pulverized and sieved through a 100-mesh sieve. The particle size distribution of the zeolite is shown in Fig. S1(a). There are about 29.4%, 79.9% and 99.6% of particles with diameters less than 5, 10 and 15 µm, respectively. Furthermore, it can be observed from Fig. S1(b) that the zeta potential of zeolite generally decreases with increasing pH. The isoelectric point (pHIEP) is 5.14, indicating a positively charged surface of the zeolite within the pH range of 1 – 5.

The particle size distribution of the zeolites and soils was measured with a particle size analyzer (Zetasizer 2000, Malvern Instruments, UK). - 1.  _Desorption and regeneration experiments_

Z@CA (3 g⋅L—1) was added to a solution containing 100 mg/L Cd(II) and shaken to achieve adsorption equilibrium. The mixture was filtered. The recyclable Z@CA was then regenerated in a solution of HCl (0.1 mol⋅L—1) followed by NaOH (0.1 mol⋅L—1) for 60 min. After filtration, the Z@CA was washed several times with distilled water to remove excess HCl and NaOH, dried, and reused to adsorb Cd(II) again. This procedure was repeated five times using the same adsorbent.

- 1.  _Pot experiments_

The tested water spinach seeds were purchased from Shouhe Co.,

Ltd.; the variety was white-stem willow leaf. The contaminated soil was collected from a paddy field in Shaoguan, Guangdong Province (113◦54′ E, 24◦68′ N), China, classified as paddy soil. It exhibits weak acidity,

which aligns with the common issue of soil acidification in agricultural regions [\[34\]](#_bookmark40). According to the soil particle size classification standard of the United States Department of Agriculture [\[35\]](#_bookmark41), the soil possesses loam texture characteristics, with volume percentages of clay, silt, and sand at 25.9%, 42.2%, and 31.9%, respectively. Additional physico-chemical properties are detailed in Table S5. Contaminated soil was placed in a plastic beaker. Z@CA was added to soil at 2.5% (w/w) while no Z@CA was added to the control (CK). For the convenience of recy-cling, the Z@CA (with individual Z@CA approach approximately 0.5 cm in length, width, and height) were packed in root bags. Then the pack-aged composites were buried in the soil surface. The experiment was

- 1.  _Characterization of Z@CA_
        1. _SEM-EDS analysis_

SEM-EDS was used to scrutinize the surface morphologies and properties of the hydrogels ([Fig. 2](#_bookmark7)). In contrast with SEM images before and after zeolite loading, it is evident that the surface of CA exhibited a relatively smooth texture devoid of conspicuous particle loading. Conversely, particulate substances were uniformly dispersed within the pores and across the surface of Z@CA. The inclusion of particles leads to a reduction in the pore structure of Z@CA. Nevertheless, some macro-porous structures can still be preserved, thereby affording sufficient space for the accommodation of water and heavy metal ions [\[38\]](#_bookmark44). In contrast to CA, obvious Si and Al signals manifested in the EDS spectrum of Z@CA and were evenly distributed on the hydrogel with a high overlay density. This observation indicated the successful integration of zeolite with CA.

- -   1.  _FT-IR and XRD analysis_

The characteristic functional groups of the zeolite, CA, and Z@CA were evaluated using FTIR spectra ([Fig. 3](#_bookmark8)a). The FTIR spectrum of the zeolite exhibited a broad peak ranging from 3714 to 3254 cm—1, attributed to the silanol group (Si-OH) stretching vibration of the zeolite and the –OH in the water molecule [\[39\]](#_bookmark45). Strong and broad characteristic peaks in the 850 — 1200 cm—1 range were attributed to symmetric and asymmetric stretching vibrations of TO4 tetrahedra (T = Si or Al) [\[40\]](#_bookmark46). The characteristic peaks of acrylamide and CMC were evident in the FTIR spectrum of CA. Specifically, the broad peak at 3555 — 3045 cm—1 was due to the stretching vibrations of –OH in CMC and –NH2 in acrylamide [\[41\]](#_bookmark47). The consecutive peaks at approximately 1647 and 1559 cm—1 correspond to C=O in amide-I and C-N in amide-II, respec-tively, indicating the presence of the –CONH2 group [\[42\]](#_bookmark48). The C=O in CMC also overlapped at 1647 cm—1, and the peak at approximately 1057 cm—1 was attributed to C-O-C stretching in CMC [\[43–45\]](#_bookmark49). In the spectrum of Z@CA, the C=O (amide I) and C-N (amide II) peaks were still readily discernible. Meanwhile, the Si-OH in zeolite partially overlapped with the –OH and –NH2 stretching vibrations in CA, result-ing in the shift of the broad peak to 3682 — 3119 cm—1. The

characteristic C-O-C peak at 1057 cm—1 and the broad peaks of Si-O and Al-O vibrations in the 850 — 1200 cm—1 range also overlapped and consequently shifted to 1105 cm—1. Based on the findings above, zeolite was effectively incorporated into the hydrogel.

The phase compositions and crystal structures of the materials were further analyzed using XRD ([Fig. 3](#_bookmark8)b). The zeolite exhibited several obvious sharp peaks at 2θ = 6.07◦, 10.0◦, 11.7◦, 15.5◦, 23.4◦, 26.8◦, 31.0◦ corresponding to the (111), (220), (400), (311), (331), (533),

(642) and (751) planes of Na-X-type zeolites (PDF#38–0237), respec-tively. CA exhibited broad, amorphous peaks in the range of 12.8◦ — 45.7◦, consistent with the findings of a previous study [\[43\]](#_bookmark49). For Z@CA, typical diffraction peaks emerged at 2θ = 6.07◦, 11.7◦, and 18.4◦, which also corresponded to the crystal structure of the Na-X zeolite. This observation provides further proof that the zeolite-loaded hydrogel composites were successfully constructed.

- -   1.  _Mechanical properties_

The mechanical properties and structural stability of Z@CA were further investigated by considering the separation and regeneration of the hydrogels in practical applications (Fig. S3). Robust mechanical properties are key prerequisites for practical applications of bulk hydrogels [\[46\]](#_bookmark50). The stress–strain curve of Z@CA exhibited characteris-tics akin to a “J” curve, demonstrating excellent mechanical strength and elasticity of the hydrogel. At a high compressive strain of 85%, Z@CA demonstrated a corresponding stress of 209.03 kPa, surpassing the mechanical strength values reported in other studies [\[47\]](#_bookmark51). The excellent mechanical properties of Z@CA may be due to the following reasons. Firstly, zeolites were incorporated as rigid particles within the three-dimensional network structure, thereby enhancing the degree of crosslinking and the flexibility of the polymer chain [\[48\]](#_bookmark52). Secondly, a double network structure was formed between the acrylamide and cel-lulose molecules. The synergistic effect of this double network can effectively absorb energy and disperse the stress on the crack into fragments, thereby enabling it to withstand greater deformation [\[49\]](#_bookmark53).

- 1.  _Adsorption behaviour_
        1. _Influence of initial pH solution_

pH is a critical parameter influencing the adsorption process due to its substantial impact on both the surface charge of the adsorbents and the morphology of heavy metals in the solution [\[50\]](#_bookmark54). As shown in [Fig. 4](#_bookmark9)a, at the initial pH of 2, the removal rate of Z@CA for Cd(II) was merely 23.52%. With an increase in pH to 3, the removal rate surged to 88.15%. When the initial pH was 4 — 7, the removal rate plateaued,

(Note: the optimal preparation parameters for Z@CA are as follows: zeolite 11.65 wt%, AM 16.95 g, MAH 5.70 g, MBA 0.1 g, CMC 2 g, KSP 0.75 g, TMEDA 250 μL, temperature 25 ◦C, mixing speed 600 rpm⋅min—1).

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 4.** (a) Adsorption capacities of Cd(II) (Ci = 100 mg⋅L—1, pHi = 2 — 7, t = 24 h) by Z@CA at different pHi values; (b) Relationship between zeta potential and pH values of Z@CA (c) Adsorption kinetics of Z@CA for Cd(II) (Ci = 100 mg⋅L—1, pHi = 5, t = 1 — 70 min) and fitting of pseudo-first-order kinetic and pseudo-second-order kinetic; (d) Intraparticle diffusion model fitting of the adsorption of Cd(II) by Z@CA; (e) Adsorption isotherms of Z@CA for Cd(II) (Ci = 5–250 mg⋅L—1, pHi = 5, t = 24 h) and fitting of Langmuir and Freundlich models; (f) Regeneration and recycle performance of the Z@CA on Cd(II).

ranging between 90.35%—90.77%. The pHIEP of Z@CA was determined to be 2.78 ([Fig. 4](#_bookmark9)b), which is lower than that of zeolite, indicating that Z@CA exhibits stronger electrostatic attraction towards cations. When the initial pH was less than 2.78, the functional groups on the surface of Z@CA were protonated, leading to a positive charge that repelled Cd(II), consequently hindering its adsorption by Z@CA [\[51,52\]](#_bookmark55). Moreover, due to the higher electronegativity of H(I) (2.1) compared to Cd(II) (1.4), H

(I) preferentially occupies the negatively charged active sites on the hydrogel surface over Cd(II) in low pH solutions, thereby further impacting adsorption [\[53\]](#_bookmark56). The zeta potential of Z@CA was negative in the pH range 3 — 6, suggesting that the deprotonation of Z@CA, resulted in a growing negative charge, thereby enhancing the electrostatic effect and adsorption capacity [\[54\]](#_bookmark57). However, the Cd(II) adsorption capacity of Z@CA was less affected by the pH in the range of 3 — 7, suggesting

that the adsorption process was not solely based on electrostatic in-teractions and that other mechanisms were also at play.

- -   1.  _Adsorption kinetics_

The experimental results for the adsorption kinetics are shown in [Fig. 4](#_bookmark9)c. The adsorption capacity of Z@CA for Cd(II) initially increased rapidly, followed by relatively slower equilibrium adsorption. After 20 min of adsorption, the adsorption capacity reached a 95% equilibrium. Subsequently, the amount of adsorbed Cd(II) increased marginally and reached an equilibrium after 50 min. The experimental data was fitted using the PFO, PSO, and Elovich equations. Compared with the other two models, the PSO model showed greater agreement between the experimental and theoretical adsorption capacities (R2 = 0.968), demonstrating that Cd(II) adsorption by Z@CA was primarily governed

by chemical adsorption.

To further explore the diffusion mechanism during Cd(II) adsorption, an intraparticle diffusion model was used ([Fig. 4](#_bookmark9)d). The findings showed that the plot of qt versus t0.5 could be divided into two linear regions representing the two stages of Cd(II) diffusion into the interior of the hydrogel. The first stage, lasting a mere five minutes, was the rapid adsorption (Ki1 = 5.3962). This can be attributed to the adsorption and diffusion of Cd(II) onto the surface of the hydrogel. The second stage was a slow adsorption stage from 5 to 70 min (Ki2 = 0.1102), dominated by chemisorption, where large amounts of active sites were consumed until adsorption equilibrium was reached [\[55\]](#_bookmark58). The intraparticle diffusion plots did not pass through the origin, indicating that intraparticle diffusion is not the sole rate-limiting process. Other processes, such as film diffusion, complexation, and ion exchange, are also involved [\[56\]](#_bookmark59).

- -   1.  _Adsorption isotherm_

[Fig. 4](#_bookmark9)e presents the results of the adsorption isotherm experiments. Generally, an escalation in adsorbate concentration corresponds to a concurrent increase in the adsorption capacity of the adsorbent. This may result from a significant localized concentration difference between the surroundings with high Cd(II) concentration and the surface of the adsorbent, thereby facilitating the Cd(II) adsorption process. As the initial concentration increased, the adsorption capacity of Z@CA steadily increased. The adsorption data were evaluated using the Freundlich and Langmuir models. The Langmuir model views the adsorption behavior of materials on the pollutants as homogeneous monolayer adsorption, whereas the Freundlich model views it as non-homogeneous multilayer adsorption [\[42\]](#_bookmark48). The obtained isotherm fitting parameters are listed in [Table 1](#_bookmark10). The Langmuir model had a higher correlation (R2 = 0.974) than the Freundlich model (R2 = 0.961), suggesting its superior aptness in delineating the Cd(II) adsorption process by Z@CA. This observation implies the uniform distribution of adsorption sites within Z@CA, consequently facilitating a homogeneous monolayer adsorption process. By fitting the Langmuir model, the maximum adsorption capacity of Z@CA for Cd(II) was calculated to be

84.4 mg⋅g—1, which is higher than that of many hydrogel composites reported in other studies [\[57,58\]](#_bookmark60). However, the adsorption capacity of Z@CA was lower than that of the zeolite in our previous study [\[25\]](#_bookmark33), due to the relatively low loading of zeolite in the hydrogel (11.65 wt%). More importantly, Z@CA could be easily recycled after application, whereas the zeolite alone could not.

- -   1.  _Reusability of Z@CA_

The reusability of an adsorbent is an important criterion for evalu-ating its performance. As depicted in [Fig. 4](#_bookmark9)f, despite undergoing five adsorption–desorption cycles, Z@CA maintained a notable Cd(II) removal efficiency of 89.88%. This can be ascribed to the stable three-dimensional network structure of the composite hydrogel, which effec-tively prevented the loss of interior active sites during repeated cycling [\[47\]](#_bookmark51). The excellent desorption, regeneration, and reusability of Z@CA make it an ideal candidate for the remediation of Cd(II)-contaminated soils.

- 1.  _Adsorption mechanisms_

To explore the potential removal mechanism of Cd(II), we investi-gated the changes in the morphology and functional groups of Z@CA

before and after Cd(II) adsorption using SEM-EDS, FTIR, and XPS.

- -   1.  _SEM-EDS analysis_

SEM-EDS analysis of Z@CA after Cd(II) adsorption is shown in [Fig. 2](#_bookmark7)g, h, and i. The surface morphology of the hydrogel underwent significant changes after adsorption. Combined with the EDS results, prominent Cd(II) signals were observed for Z@CA after adsorption, confirming the successful capture of Cd(II) by Z@CA. Concurrently, the Na content decreased from 3% to 0.4%. The Na in Z@CA originated primarily from the CMC and zeolite. In the zeolite, O functioned as a “bridge,” linking Si or Si and Al within the aluminosilicate framework structure, while Na occupied the pore structure in ionic form to maintain charge equilibrium [\[51\]](#_bookmark55). Previous studies have shown that the primary mechanism of Cd(II) adsorption by these zeolites involves ion exchange with Na(I) [\[25\]](#_bookmark33). Considering the variation in the Na content before and after adsorption, it can be inferred that ion exchange also occurred during Cd(II) adsorption by Z@CA.

- -   1.  _XPS and FTIR analysis_

XPS was used to monitor the functional group changes in Z@CA before and after Cd(II) adsorption and the distribution of Cd(II) on the hydrogel. As shown in [Fig. 5](#_bookmark11)a, the wide-scan survey XPS spectra revealed that the Z@CA hydrogel was predominantly composed of Na, O, N, C, Si, and Al. Following adsorption, the characteristic orbital of Cd was detected, along with an obvious reduction in the Na peak. These findings implied that the adsorption process involved ion exchange be-tween Cd(II) and Na(I) [\[59,60\]](#_bookmark61). The detailed survey of the Cd 3d ([Fig. 5](#_bookmark11)b) could be resolved into two characteristic peaks located at

405.89 and 412.62 eV, corresponding to Cd 3d3/2 and Cd 3d5/2, respectively. Notably, the binding energy of the Cd 3d5/2 main peak is

404.8 eV [\[61\]](#_bookmark62). In this study, the binding energy of the Cd 3d5/2 main peak was 405.89 eV, indicating the coordination of Cd(II) not only with oxygen-containing functional groups but also with nitrogen-containing groups [\[61\]](#_bookmark62). This implies the complex adsorption behavior of Cd(II) on Z@CA, with the adsorption process likely involving complexation between the amino/oxygen functionalities and Cd(II).

[Fig. 5](#_bookmark11)c — f shows narrow-spectrum scans of Na 1 s, O 1 s, Si 2p, and Al 2p to validate the adsorption mechanism further. It could be observed that after adsorption, the intensity of the Na 1 s peak was markedly reduced, and the binding energy increased from 1071.94 to 1072.22 eV. Additionally, the Na Auger peak at 536.68 eV in the O 1 s spectrum declined after Cd(II) adsorption, which is consistent with the EDS re-sults. Moreover, the binding energy of the characteristic Si 2p and Al 2p peaks increased by 0.22 and 0.27 eV after adsorption. This may be attributed to the smaller hydrated ionic radius of Cd (275 Å) compared to Na (2.99 Å), the available adsorption surface of the hydrated cad-mium ion was larger than that of the hydrated sodium ion. The replacement of Na(I) by Cd(II) compressed the spatial structure of the zeolite in the hydrogel, lowering the electron cloud density [\[25\]](#_bookmark33). These analyses confirm that ion exchange occurred during Cd(II) adsorption by Z@CA.

The XPS of O 1 s showed values of 530.97 and 531.77 eV that are reported for C=O and C-O. After the reaction, the two peaks shifted to

531.05 and 531.97 eV, respectively, indicating the involvement of these oxygen-containing functional groups in the adsorption. The O in the organic group can form coordinated covalent bonds with heavy metals, thus lowering the electron cloud density around the O and generating

**Fig. 5.** XPS spectra of Z@CA before and after Cd(II) adsorption: (a) survey-scan spectra, (b) Cd 3d spectra, (c) Na 1 s spectra, (d) O 1 s spectra, (e) Si 2p spectra, (f) Al 2p spectra, (g) N 1 s spectra and (h) C 1 s spectra.

Cd-O bonds [\[62\]](#_bookmark63). This results in a positive shift in the binding energy [\[63\]](#_bookmark64). For the N 1 s spectrum ([Fig. 5](#_bookmark11)g), the binding energy of –NH2 increased from 399.52 to 400.09 eV after adsorption, which can be attributed to the fact that the lone pair of electrons on the N being donated to Cd(II) to form coordinate bonds during adsorption, resulting in a decrease in its electron cloud density and an increase in binding energy [\[64\]](#_bookmark65). The C 1 s spectrum ([Fig. 5](#_bookmark11)h) exhibited three contributions: C-C at 284.80 eV, C-N at 285.68 eV, and C=O at 288.81 eV. After adsorption, the binding energies of the C-N and C=O specific peaks were shifted to higher energies by 0.72 and 0.20 eV, respectively. The binding energy of C-C remained unchanged after adsorption. The significant increase in the binding energies of C-N and C=O can be ascribed to re-actions between the adjacent N and O atoms and metal ions [\[65,66\]](#_bookmark66). These results indicate that –NH2, C=O, C-O, and C-N are involved in Cd

(II) adsorption by Z@CA and serve as primary binding sites. These functional groups can immobilize Cd(II) via complexation or chelation reactions. At the same time, a comparison of the FTIR of Z@CA before and after Cd(II) adsorption revealed shifts in the characteristic peak positions of –NH2, C=O, and C-N located at 3421.56, 1647, and 1559 cm—1 to 3436.13, 1644, and 1554 cm—1, respectively. This further val-idates the involvement of nitrogen- and oxygen-containing groups in the hydrogel during Cd(II) adsorption.

- 1.  _Performance of the Z@CA as soil amendment_
        1. _Effect of Z@CA on soil pH, bioavailable Cd(II) and total Cd(II)_

As shown in [Table 2](#_bookmark12), compared to the original soil, there was no significant change in the concentration of bioavailable Cd(II) in the CK soil (_p_ \> 0.05). However, following the application of Z@CA, there was a significant decrease of 59.38% in the concentration of bioavailable Cd

(II) (p ≤ 0.05). Soil pH is an important factor affecting the speciation and mobility of heavy metals in soil. Compared to the original soil, the pH significantly increased by 10.84% (_p_ ≤ 0.05) after the application of Z@CA. The higher pH value was conducive to the adsorption and pre-cipitation of heavy metals in the soil [\[67,68\]](#_bookmark67). Meanwhile, the total Cd(II)

content of the CK soil exhibited no significant change before and after the experiment (_p_ \> 0.05), while there was a significant decrease of 1.75% after the application of Z@CA (_p_ < 0.05). Experiments in aqueous solutions demonstrated the excellent adsorption capacity of Z@CA for

Cd(II). Nevertheless, the Cd(II) removal efficiency in soil environments is relatively low. This inconsistency could stem from the lower con-centration of Cd(II) (2.343 mg⋅kg—1) in the contaminated soil compared to the aqueous solution (100 mg⋅kg—1), thus significantly reducing the probability of Cd(II) exposure to the adsorbents. Additionally, the bioavailable fraction was 68.29%, with 31.72% of the Cd(II) present in a relatively stable state, which is not conducive to the direct adsorption of Cd(II) by Z@CA. Nevertheless, Z@CA demonstrates promising potential as a material for the removal of heavy metals. It reduced both the bioavailable Cd(II) content and the total Cd(II) content in the soil.

- -   1.  _Effect of Z@CA on the growth of water spinach_

Water spinach exhibits a high capacity to accumulate Cd(II) [\[69,70\]](#_bookmark68). The Cd(II) content in the aerial parts of water spinach from CK was 1.40

mg⋅kg—1 ([Table. 2](#_bookmark12)), surpassing the Chinese risk control value of 0.2 mg⋅kg—1 (GB 2762–2022). However, after the application of Z@CA, the Cd(II) content in the aerial parts of the water spinach was significantly reduced by 91.43% (_p_ < 0.05), falling below the control value. A comparative analysis was also conducted on the weight, height, and

relative chlorophyll content of the aerial parts of water spinach under the two treatments. A digital photo of water spinaches is shown in [Fig. 6](#_bookmark13). Water spinach under the CK treatment exhibited relatively stunted growth, with an average height of 14.27 cm in the aerial part. In contrast, water spinach showed robust growth, with an average height of 19.06 cm, 1.34 times that of CK after the application of Z@CA.

Simultaneously, the application of Z@CA led to a significant increase in the fresh weight of the aerial parts of water spinach (_p_ < 0.05), reaching

1.73 times that of CK. The relative chlorophyll content reflects the level

of photosynthesis in plants, with higher values indicating vigorous metabolic activity [\[71\]](#_bookmark69). In comparison to the control (CK), the appli-cation of Z@CA led to a significant increase of 48.67% (_p_ < 0.05) in the

relative chlorophyll content of water spinach, which was more favorable

for maintaining chlorophyll levels in a Cd(II)-contaminated environ-ment. Based on these results, it can be inferred that Z@CA effectively alleviated the toxic effects of Cd(II) on the growth of water spinach to a significant extent.

- -   1.  _Recovery of Z@CA_

After harvesting the water spinach, all Z@CA was recovered and analyzed by quantitative calculations to explore its recovery efficiency and resistance to degradation. As shown in [Table 2](#_bookmark12), the recovery effi-ciency of Z@CA was as high as 94.77%, leaving minimal residue in the soil. Moreover, the digital photo of Z@CA after recycling (Fig. S4) cor-roborates the preservation of its intact structure. The robust mechanical strength of Z@CA enables it to withstand soil compression without fragmentation. The high recovery efficiency was attributed to the min-imal degradation of the hydrogel in the soil, highlighting its consider-able environmental stability.

# Conclusions

This study demonstrated that Z@CA, produced by loading zeolite into hydrogel, has the potential to remove Cd(II) from the soil. The adsorption experiments demonstrated that Z@CA exhibited excellent adsorption capacity for Cd(II) (84.4 mg⋅g—1), the electrostatic in-teractions, ion exchange, and complexation between Cd(II) and the functional groups (–NH2, C=O, C-O, and C-N) enhanced the removal efficiency of Cd(II). After five adsorption–desorption cycles, Z@CA still showed good renewability. Z@CA also processes strong mechanical properties (compressive stress of 209.03 kPa at 85% strain), enabling it to effectively withstand soil compression. After applying Z@CA in the Cd(II)-contaminated soil, Z@CA can be largely recovered with a rate of

94.77 % and maintain its original intact structure. Meanwhile, the content of both available Cd(II) (59.38%) and total Cd(II) (1.75%) in soil decreased significantly. Z@CA also effectively alleviated the toxic ef-fects of Cd(II) on water spinach. The Cd(II) content of water spinach was significantly reduced by 91.43%, and the weight, height, and relative
